# What $\approx_{\mathcal A}$ Remembers

The congruence at the core of the complementation proof does **not** remember the exact word. For a finite word $u$ it remembers only, for every pair of states $(p,q)$:

- whether some path labelled $u$ goes from $p$ to $q$ at all, and
- if so, whether such a path can **visit an accepting state** along the way.

This is a finite **profile** — a grid over $Q\times Q$ with entries in $\{-,\ q,\ q^{F}\}$:

- $-$ : **no path** from $p$ to $q$ labelled $u$;
- $q$ : a path reaches $q$, but **without** visiting $F$;
- $q^{F}$ : a path reaches $q$ **visiting** an accepting state.

Two words are **$\approx_{\mathcal A}$-equivalent** exactly when they have the *same grid*. There are finitely many grids, so $\approx_{\mathcal A}$ has finite index — and it saturates $L(\mathcal A)$. The automaton $\mathcal A$ used here (from the chapter) accepts the $\omega$-words in which the block $ab$ occurs infinitely often, separated by $c$'s. Note $\Delta$ is **partial**: a missing transition means the run has nowhere to go, not a sink.

```{=html}
<script>
(function(){
  const States=['s0','s1','s2']; const Fset=new Set(['s1']);
  const Delta=[['s0','a','s1'],['s1','b','s2'],['s2','c','s2'],['s2','a','s1']];
  const NONE=0,REACH=1,REACHF=2;
  const empty=()=>{const P={};States.forEach(p=>{P[p]={};States.forEach(q=>P[p][q]=NONE);});return P;};
  function base(sym){const P=empty();Delta.forEach(([p,x,q])=>{if(x===sym){const v=(Fset.has(p)||Fset.has(q))?REACHF:REACH;if(v>P[p][q])P[p][q]=v;}});return P;}
  function ident(){const P=empty();States.forEach(p=>P[p][p]=Fset.has(p)?REACHF:REACH);return P;}
  function compose(R,S){const T=empty();for(const p of States)for(const r of States){if(R[p][r]===NONE)continue;for(const q of States){if(S[r][q]===NONE)continue;const v=(R[p][r]===REACHF||S[r][q]===REACHF)?REACHF:REACH;if(v>T[p][q])T[p][q]=v;}}return T;}
  function profile(w){let P=ident();for(const ch of w)P=compose(P,base(ch));return P;}
  const parse=s=>s.trim().replace(/\s|,/g,'').split('').filter(x=>x.length);
  const sub=q=>'s<sub>'+q[1]+'</sub>';
  function gridHTML(P){
    let h='<table class="grid"><tr><th>p \\ q</th>'+States.map(q=>`<th>${sub(q)}</th>`).join('')+'</tr>';
    for(const p of States){
      h+=`<tr><th>${sub(p)}</th>`;
      for(const q of States){
        const v=P[p][q];
        if(v===NONE) h+='<td class="cell-none">&minus;</td>';
        else if(v===REACH) h+=`<td class="cell-reach">${sub(q)}</td>`;
        else h+=`<td class="cell-reachF">${sub(q)}<sup>F</sup></td>`;
      }
      h+='</tr>';
    }
    return h+'</table>';
  }
  function eq(A,B){return States.every(p=>States.every(q=>A[p][q]===B[p][q]));}
  function go(){
    const w1=parse(document.getElementById('nb21-w1').value), w2=parse(document.getElementById('nb21-w2').value);
    for(const w of [w1,w2]) for(const s of w) if(!['a','b','c'].includes(s)){document.getElementById('nb21-verdict').innerHTML=`<div class='verdict-box verdict-fail'>Unknown symbol "${s}". Alphabet is {a,b,c}.</div>`;return;}
    const P1=profile(w1),P2=profile(w2);
    document.getElementById('nb21-t1').innerHTML='profile("'+(w1.join('')||'ε')+'")';
    document.getElementById('nb21-t2').innerHTML='profile("'+(w2.join('')||'ε')+'")';
    document.getElementById('nb21-g1').innerHTML=gridHTML(P1);
    document.getElementById('nb21-g2').innerHTML=gridHTML(P2);
    const same=eq(P1,P2);
    document.getElementById('nb21-verdict').innerHTML=`<div class="verdict-box ${same?'verdict-pass':'verdict-fail'}"><strong>"${w1.join('')||'ε'}" ${same?'≈𝒜':'≉𝒜'} "${w2.join('')||'ε'}"</strong> — the two grids are ${same?'identical, so the words are indistinguishable to 𝒜':'different (some cell disagrees), so 𝒜 can tell them apart'}.</div>`;
  }
  document.getElementById('nb21-preset').addEventListener('change',()=>{
    const pairs=[['c','ab'],['ab','abc'],['abc','abcc'],['a','ba'],['','cc']][+document.getElementById('nb21-preset').value];
    document.getElementById('nb21-w1').value=pairs[0]; document.getElementById('nb21-w2').value=pairs[1]; go();
  });
  document.getElementById('nb21-go').addEventListener('click',go);
  ['nb21-w1','nb21-w2'].forEach(id=>document.getElementById(id).addEventListener('keyup',e=>{if(e.key==='Enter')go();}));
  go();
})();
</script>
```

The default pair reproduces the chapter's example: for $u=c$ the only non-trivial cell is $(s_2,s_2)=s_2$ (a $c$-loop that never touches $F$), whereas for $u=ab$ two cells carry $F$, at $(s_0,s_2)$ and $(s_2,s_2)$ — the path $s_0\!\to\!s_1\!\to\!s_2$ visits $s_1\in F$. Different cells at the same position, so $c\not\approx_{\mathcal A}ab$. Try `abc` vs `abcc`: **equal** grids — the extra $c$ just loops at $s_2$, which is why every block $ab\,c^{i}$ falls in one class (the key fact behind **[Notebook 23](23-ramsey-decomposition.qmd)**).
